paragraphs: Farmer John is planning to open a new university for cows!

There are N (1 ≤ N ≤ 10⁵) cows who could potentially attend this university. Each cow is willing to pay a maximum tuition of cᵢ (1 ≤ cᵢ ≤ 10⁶). Farmer John can set the tuition that all cows must pay to enroll. If this tuition is greater than the maximum a cow is willing to pay, then the cow will not attend the university.
Farmer John wants to make the most possible money so he can pay his instructors a fair wage. Please determine how much money he can make, and how much tuition he should charge.
inputFormat: The second line contains N integers c₁, c₂, …, cₙ, where cᵢ is the maximum tuition cow i is willing to pay.
outputFormat: Please output the maximum amount of money Farmer John can make and the optimal tuition he should charge. If there are multiple solutions, output the solution with the smallest optimal tuition.
Note that the large size of integers involved in this problem may require the use of 64-bit integer data types (e.g., a "long" in Java, a "long long" in C/C++).

sampleExplanation.title: Sample Analysis
sampleExplanation.detail: If Farmer John charges a tuition of 4, then 3 cows (those willing to pay 6, 4, and 6) will attend, earning 3 × 4 = 12. Charging 6 only attracts 2 cows for 2 × 6 = 12, and 4 is smaller than 6.
sampleExplanation.steps: Sorted c = [1, 4, 6, 6]  →  tuition 4 × 3 cows = 12 (smallest optimal tuition)

hints.title: Which Tuition Values Could Be Optimal?
hints.body: Suppose Farmer John picks a tuition T that is strictly between two cows' limits. He could raise T up to the next cow's limit without losing any students! So the optimal tuition is always equal to one of the cᵢ values.

hints.title: Sort the Maximum Tuitions
hints.body: Sort the array c in non-decreasing order: c₀ ≤ c₁ ≤ … ≤ cₙ₋₁. Now, if you test setting the tuition to c[i], every cow from index i to N − 1 is willing to pay at least c[i]!

hints.title: Count Attending Cows & Watch 64-bit Overflow
hints.body: When sorted left-to-right, setting tuition = c[i] brings in (N − i) cows (as long as we consider the first occurrence or note that a smaller index i for the same value gives a larger N − i). Track bestRevenue < revenue (strictly greater!) when scanning from smallest tuition to largest so ties automatically keep the smallest tuition. Remember N × cᵢ can reach 10¹¹, so use long long in C++ and long in Java!

editorial.summary: Sort c in ascending order. Scanning i from 0 to N − 1, if Farmer John charges c[i], then at least (N − i) cows can afford it, yielding revenue (N − i) · c[i]. Updating only when revenue strictly exceeds bestRevenue naturally breaks ties in favor of the smallest tuition.
editorial.complexity: Time: O(N log N)  |  Space: O(N)

solutions.python:
import sys

def solve():
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.read().split()))
    n = data[0]
    c = sorted(data[1:1 + n])
    best_rev = -1
    best_tuition = 0
    for i, tuition in enumerate(c):
        rev = tuition * (n - i)
        if rev > best_rev:
            best_rev = rev
            best_tuition = tuition
    print(f"{best_rev} {best_tuition}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    solve()
